full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-respondent Haque Brother (Industries) Ltd. filed the aforesaid suit for permanent injunction on the averments, inter alia, that it is one of the leading manufacturers of biscuits in Bangladesh. In 1979 the plaintiff invented a new type of biscuit first of its kind in Bangladesh by using high protein. The plaintiff also invented a new design to be applied to such biscuits. The plaintiff also adopted the word "Mr. COOKIE", the word "HAQUE," inside a panel and the monogram of the letters HB with the device of CRESCENT and STAR with a particular colour of design and get-up printed on a carton as their Trade Mark. The plaintiff also registered the said Trade Mark, Patent, Design and Copyright with the Registrar of Trade Mark, the Controller of Patents and Designs and the Registrar of Copyrights respectively. By virtue of the said registration with the appropriate authorities the plaintiff has became the absolute owner of the said Trade Mark, Parent, Design and Copyright in Bangladesh and nobody else in Bangladesh has any right to use the same for biscuits. The plaintiff has also given wide publicity of their said Trade Mark by various publicity media. The said biscuit has become very popular in the market. Out of greed and sheer business jealousy the defendant M/s A.B. Biscuit Co. Ltd. has very recently started a biscuit manufacturing business and they have infringed, counterfeited, forged, imitated and pirated the said registered Trade Mark, Patent, Design and Copyright of the plaintiff. The plaintiff by notice asked the defendant to stop forthwith the production of the imitated biscuits but they did not. Hence this suit for permanent injunction restraining the defendant, its servants and agents from producing or selling any biscuits with the Trade Mark. Patent, Design and Copyright of the plaintiff as given in Schedules A and C of the plaint or any other mark or marks design or designs which directly conflict with or resemble the Trade Mark and Design of the plaintiff. 

 3. The plaintiff-respondent also filed an application under Order 39, rule 2 C.P.C. praying for temporary injunction in the above terms till the disposal of the suit and as stated above obtained an order of ad interim injunction from the learned District Judge on 27.10.81. 

 4. The defendant-appellant filed a written objection denying the material allegations of the plaintiff-respondent. It is the case of the defendant-appellant that the specimens of the respective cartons of the plaintiff and the defendant have their different and distinctive features. There is no resemblance between the two so as to deceive an unwary customer. The defendant's carton bears the name "King Cookie" with a picture of crown along with letters 'AB' printed in English as well as in Bengali in a different type and design. In the defendant's caution there is no mention of the word "HAQUE" and there is no carton of a man with a hat in hand as printed on the carton of the plaintiff There is nothing resembling the picture and devices of CRESCENT AND STAR with the monogram of letters within the black base of a triangle which are, according to the plaintiff, the distinguishing and essential features of their Trade Mark. The defendant contended that the word "Cookie" is an English word of Scotch origin, the meaning of which is, according to the Concise Oxford Dictionary, "Plain Bun", "small flat Cake", "Biscuit". The defendant contended that there cannot be any special distinctiveness in the use of the word "Cookie" in different variety of biscuits. The defendant has also used the English word "SYMBOL OF INTERNATIONAL QUALITY" and the Bengali words "which are printed round the picture of a (lower in the form of an arc. The Patent and Design of the defendant's "KING COOKIE" have also no resemblance whatsoever with those of the plaintiff's "MR. COOKIE". The defendant also pointed out other differences between the plaintiff's carton and the defendant's carton. 

 5. In a short judgment the learned District Judge has held that the plaintiff's and defendant's cartons are both of yellow colour on a red background. Prima facie the illiterate and unwary customers are not expected to distinguish between the two. He also held that prima facie the defendant's biscuits are colourable imitation of the registered Trade Mark under which the plaintiffs are manufacturing the "Mr. Cookie butter coconut biscuits". The plaintiff's monetary loss cannot be ascertained. So they will suffer irreparable loss in the absence of the Court's protection. Hence the order of ad interim injunction date 27.10.81 was made absolute. 

 6. The certificate of Trade Mark registration shows that the entire carton, but not any particular part thereof, has been registered with the registrar of Trade Marks on 30.11.79. The Design registered under the Patents and Designs Act, 1911 is not in respect of the carton but in respect of the biscuit itself. A photograph of the design of the biscuit of the plaintiff is contained in schedule 'C' of the plaint and a photograph of the design of the biscuit of the defendant is contained in schedule 'D' of the plaint. Prima facie the biscuits are of different shapes and configurations and as such in this case the question of imitating the Design of the biscuit itself and infringing the Design of the plaintiff does not arise. As far as the Copyright is concerned the plaintiff has obtained the Copyright of "Mr. Cookie Butter Coconut" biscuit carton on 18.9.80 from the Registrar of Copyright, Government of Bangladesh. 

 7. In this appeal Mr. Abdur Rashid Khan, the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant has taken me through the two cartons of the plaintiff and the defendant and has emphasised the various differences in the monogram, get-up, design, lettering, symbol, configuration, etc. in the two cartons. In a case of imitation, however, no two cartons are exactly alike. There is bound to be some difference here and there. But taking the two cartons, not side by side which is not a proper method of comparison in such cases, but by looking at one at one time and then looking at another, there can be no doubt prima facie that an unwary customer is likely to be deceived and confused by the similarities of shape, size, colour-combination and get-up of the cartons. This is not to say that there are no differences between the two cartons but in spite of the differences the over-all impression is one of imitation. The defendant-appellant certainly could have devised some other colour combinations, get-up, size and shape to popularise its own version of biscuits produced among other ingredients with butter and coconut. 

 8. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent has submitted that the word "Mr. COOKIE" is the plaintiff's part of Trade Mark and as long as he has the registered proprietorship over the Trade Mark, no one else can use this word. Mr. Abdur Rashid Khan's reply is two fold: first, the plaintiff has not taken any special registration in respect of a particular portion of the entire carton. Secondly, the word "COOKIE" is merely descriptive and not fancy one. He has cited the case of McCain International Ltd. Vs. Country Fair Foods Ltd. and another, 1981 R.P.C. (Reports of Patent Design and Trade Mark Cases) 69 (CA) in support of his submission. 

 9. In the aforecited case the facts are that in the beginning of 1979 the plaintiffs introduced on to the U.K. market a novel product—chips which could be cooked in the oven or baked under the grill—and sold the product under the name "McCain Oven Chips". In April 1980 the defendants sought to launch their version of the product under the names "Country Fair Oven Chips" and "Birds Eye Oven Chips". The plaintiffs obtained an ex-parte injunction in the Queen's Bench Division to restrain the defendants from marketing their product under the name "Oven Chips" whether with or without their own names and at the hearing inter parts the injunction was continued until judgment. The defendants appealed before the Court of Appeal. The defendants contended the name "Oven Chips" was descriptive of the product, that it had not subsequently acquired distinctiveness and that where a descriptive name had been applied to a product by the sole supplier of that product that came could not easily acquire distinctiveness. The plaintiffs argued that "Oven Chips" was not descriptive but was a fancy name being an ungrammatical combination of two words which had not previously been associated together and further that by virtue of the plaintiff's extensive sales and advertising it had become distinctive of their product. Allowing the appeal it was held by the Court of Appeal that the plaintiffs having consistently advertised and sold their product under the name ‘'McCain Oven Chips", this was strong evidence that the name ''Oven Chips" was descriptive of the product and the name "McCain" indicated the source of origin of the product. It was also held that the name "Oven Chips" was an ingenious and apt description of the product, although the consumer could not have become aware of what the expression meant until the product came on the market: once on the market the name "Oven Chips" would inform the consumer of the nature of the product. It was also held that while a descriptive term may acquire a secondary meaning, the period in the present case was far too short for such a secondary meaning to have been acquired, particularly in view of the plaintiffs constant reference to their product as "McCain Oven Chips". It was also held that where a person introduces a new product to the market, gives it a name descriptive of the product and has a monopoly, whether legal or de facto, in that product, he cannot claim a monopoly in that name. He can only require that other persons who make the same product distinguish their products by appropriate means. The defendants had done this by making it clear that their products came from Country Fair and Birds Eye respectively. 

 10. In the present case it is the case of the plaintiff that the new type of biscuits known as Cookie was invented by the plaintiff in 1979. The relevant registrations were obtained in the years 1979 and 1980. The word 'Cookie' is obviously a descriptive name which occupies a place in the Concise Oxford Dictionary. It means "Plain Bun", "Small flat Cake" "Biscuit". The word 'Cookie' therefore is descriptive of the product. The plaintiff does not call its product as simple 'Cookie', but 'Mr. Cookie'. The constant reference to their product as 'Mr. Cookie' prima facie suggests that the descriptive term has not yet acquired a secondary meaning and in any case the period of production of 'Mr. Cookie' biscuits in the present case is far too short for a secondary meaning to have been acquired. The defendant in order to distinguish its product from that of the plaintiff has named its product as "King Cookie". Adopting the reasons of the decision reported in 1981 R.P.O. 69, therefore, it appears that although the plaintiff has introduced a new product to the market and has given a name descriptive of the product and has a mono-poly in that product, he cannot claim a monopoly in that name. He can only require that other persons who make the same product distinguish their products by appropriate means. 

 11. In the case reported in 198! R.P.C. 69 it was held that the defendants distinguished their products by appropriate means. In the instant case I have already held that the defendant appellant has prima facie failed to do so. Agreeing with the learned District Judge I hold that the colour combination and general get-up in the two cartons of both the parties are likely to confuse the ordinary and unwary customers. The plaintiff has a prima facie arguable case in the suit. The plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury if under the circumstances they are not protected by the Court. The balance of inconveniences under the circumstances are less in favour of the plaintiff. As such their prayer for temporary injunction was rightly, granted by the learned District Judge. 

 13. The avoid any misunderstanding, it is specifically directed that the trial Court must totally ignore the views of this Court with regard to temporary injunction. The suit will be decided completely on the evidence on record and on the appreciation of facts and law independently by the trial Court without being influenced in any way by any prima facie finding or observation on the issue of temporary injunction in this judgment.
